opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and honestly the term gets thrown around so loosely right now that it's worth being precise about it. The way I think about it, the core distinction is between a system where the developer decides the control flow and a system where the model decides the control flow.

In a traditional LLM application, even a pretty sophisticated one, you as the engineer write out the steps: retrieve some documents, stuff them into a prompt, call the model, maybe parse the output and call it again. The model is a component, but the logic of what happens next lives in your code. An agentic system flips that. You give the model a goal, a set of tools it can use, and some environment it can observe, and then the model itself decides what to do next, whether to search, write code, ask a clarifying question, try something different because the last attempt failed, or decide it's done.

So the practical markers I look for are: it operates in a loop over multiple steps, it takes actions through tools that actually affect something, it observes the results of those actions and adapts, and it has some notion of when the task is complete. The longer the horizon and the more open-ended the decisions, the more agentic it is. I think of it as a spectrum more than a binary.

The reason the distinction matters, beyond semantics, is that it changes how you build and evaluate these things. When the model owns the control flow, you can't just test individual prompts anymore. You have to think about trajectories, about failure recovery, about how errors compound over many steps. That's where a lot of the interesting and hard engineering work is right now.

r001.rationale: The response describes multi-step operation and says longer horizons are more agentic, but it does not identify tasks taking longer than a few seconds as a defining feature.

r002.rationale: It mentions using tools that affect something and observing an environment, but does not clearly identify interacting with the real world to solve the user's problem as a defining feature.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is one of those terms that gets thrown around a lot and means something slightly different to everyone, so let me give you the way I think about it.

The simplest definition I use is: an agentic system is one where the language model gets to decide what happens next. In a traditional LLM application, you as the developer write the control flow. You say, first call the model to classify the query, then retrieve some documents, then call the model again to synthesize an answer. The model is doing work at each step, but the structure of the program is fixed by you ahead of time. In an agentic system, you hand some of that control over to the model. You give it a set of tools, you give it a goal, and it decides which tools to call, in what order, how many times, and when it's done.

So I think of it less as a binary and more as a spectrum. On one end you have a single prompt, single completion. A little further along you have chains and workflows, where there's maybe some branching but the developer still owns the structure. Then you get to systems where the model is in a loop, observing the results of its actions and planning the next one. The further you move along that spectrum, the more autonomy the model has, and the more the behavior of the system depends on the model's judgment rather than on code you wrote.

The reason I like that framing is that it tells you something practical about what gets hard. The more control you give the model, the more the range of possible behaviors explodes, and the harder it gets to test, to evaluate, to guarantee anything about the outcome. A lot of the engineering of building these systems is really about figuring out how much autonomy is actually warranted for the task, and building the scaffolding around it so that when the model makes a bad call, you can catch it and recover.

And I'd add one more piece, which is that the interesting agents are the ones that take actions in the world, not just produce text. Writing and executing code, browsing a website, calling an API, modifying files. Once the model can do things with side effects, that's when it really starts to feel like an agent rather than a chatbot with extra steps, and it's also when the stakes of getting it wrong go up.

r001.rationale: The response discusses autonomy, tool use, and repeated action, but does not identify working on tasks longer than a few seconds as a defining feature.

r002.rationale: It says agents take actions in the world, such as browsing, calling APIs, and modifying files, and contrasts this with producing text alone.

astra-6.text:
I think of an agentic AI system as a system where an LLM is making decisions about how to accomplish a task, rather than just generating a response. You give it a goal, and it can decide what action to take, use a tool, observe the result, and then decide what to do next.

And I think agentic is more of a spectrum than a binary distinction. At one end, you have a predefined workflow with an LLM doing a few steps. At the other, you give the system a high-level objective and let it figure out the steps itself. The more control the model has over that process, the more agentic I'd call the system.

r001.rationale: The response describes choosing and repeating actions toward a goal, but does not identify working on tasks longer than a few seconds as a defining feature.

r002.rationale: It mentions using tools and observing results, but does not identify interaction with the real world to solve the user's problem as a defining feature.
